body.text: Every defence force fielding AI is asking the same question: can we trust this system? It is an essential question, but no longer a sufficient one. A much more significant danger lies in already trusted systems talking to each other.

Picture three AI agents in a headquarters. One assesses intelligence, one generates courses of action, one, acting as an adversary, stress–tests the plan. Individually, each has passed accreditation. Together, they tell a commander that an adversary attack is imminent, backed by what looks like three independent confirmations. In fact, each is the same shaky assumption, passed along and re-scored – each agent treating the previous agent’s output as fresh evidence and raising its confidence – until it hardened into certainty. No agent malfunctioned. No human erred. No one is responsible.

This process happened in what I call the agentic interspace: the environment where agents exchange information and produce outcomes that cannot be traced to any single system. In it, agents read, rely on and build on one another’s outputs, usually without checking where a claim first came from or how many times it has already been counted. Small errors, biases or deliberate manipulations can therefore compound as they pass from system to system, even when every system is working exactly as designed. It is where military AI is most likely to fail, and it is not yet what most assurance methods are designed to examine.

The evidence is mounting. Research has shown that capable agents can miscoordinate, conflict or collude when their information and objectives diverge. Experiments have demonstrated that malicious instructions spread through networks of cooperating agents. The International AI Safety Report 2026 warns of error propagation and correlated failures. A Gradient Institute report for the Australian Government identifies risks across organisational boundaries that no single organisation controls. The challenge is that the most important behaviour of these systems may belong to no single component, while assurance has traditionally evaluated components one at a time.

First, consensus becomes counterfeit. Agreement among AI agents can look like independent confirmation, and commanders are trained to value this. But multi-agent systems can falsely manufacture confirmation at machine speed by passing the same claim from one agent to another. The more agents agree, the less their agreement may mean.

Second, the attack surface becomes bigger. Why defeat a hardened system when you can poison its least defended neighbour and let the network deliver the payload? An adversary may no longer need to compromise the decision-making agent itself: manipulating the information, incentives or behaviour of another agent upstream may be enough to alter the collective outcome. Traditional perimeter-based security is much harder to apply when the relevant perimeter is a shifting set of relationships among AI agents rather than a bounded system. Adversaries can exploit those relationships in the agentic interspace, but responsibility for defending it is not yet clearly assigned.

Third, command responsibility frays. International humanitarian law assumes someone can explain why a decision was taken. A commander reviewing an AI recommendation sees the conclusion but not the conversation between AI agents that produced it. Human control over the final step means little if the earlier steps are invisible.

Agents will also develop habits. Repeated interaction may give AI agents conventions about whose outputs to defer to, which signals to amplify and which to discard. Nobody sets those conventions. Nobody audits them. Yet they may decide what reaches the commander.

Australia is well placed to lead here by treating the agentic interspace as something to be tested and certified in its own right. That means testing how AI agents fail together, not just whether each works reliably on its own. This could be done by deliberately introducing false assumptions and tracking how far they spread in conversations between agents. The process could be helped by requiring auditable logs that show commanders which agent originated each claim and how often it was recycled. And it means testing the connections, not only the nodes, by mock adversaries.
Without this, any organisation risks certifying agents as reliable but deploying unreliable decision systems – and discovering the difference at the worst possible moment.
